---
title: "Lecture 11: Interest-Rate Options"
subtitle: "Use asymmetric payoffs to reshape fixed-income risk"
author: "BUS 411"
---

## Options turn rate risk into a choice

> The buyer pays a premium for a **right without an obligation**.

- Calls protect or benefit from higher underlying prices
- Puts protect or benefit from lower underlying prices
- The seller receives premium and accepts contingent exposure

Options reshape the distribution rather than simply reversing direction.

## Calls and puts allocate exercise rights

| Contract | Buyer may… | Exercise when… |
|---|---|---|
| Call | Buy at strike $K$ | Underlying price is high |
| Put | Sell at strike $K$ | Underlying price is low |

The buyer chooses; the writer must perform if assigned.

- **European:** exercise only at expiration
- **American:** exercise any time through expiration

American flexibility cannot reduce option value, but early exercise is not always optimal.

## Futures create symmetry; options create asymmetry

| Position | Upside | Downside | Upfront premium |
|---|---|---|---|
| Long futures | Unlimited | Unlimited | No option premium |
| Long call | Unlimited | Limited to premium | Yes |
| Long put | Large if price falls | Limited to premium | Yes |

Margin and daily settlement still matter for futures and many option-writing positions.

## Interest-rate options appear in several forms

- Options on cash bonds
- Caps and floors on interest rates
- Swaptions
- Options on Treasury or SOFR futures
- Embedded calls and puts in bonds

The underlying and settlement convention determine how a rate move becomes an option payoff.

- Exercise a futures call → receive a long futures position
- Exercise a futures put → receive a short futures position

Most exchange-traded positions are closed or offset rather than exercised into delivery.

## Treasury futures option premiums use 64ths

Premium quote 0-40 means:

$$\frac{40}{64}=0.625\text{ points}$$

With \$1,000 per full point:

$$0.625(\$1{,}000)=\$625$$

Do not confuse the option premium convention with the futures price convention in 32nds.

## Intrinsic value is the value of immediate exercise

$$C_{intrinsic}=\max(S-K,0)$$

$$P_{intrinsic}=\max(K-S,0)$$

| Position | In the money when… |
|---|---|
| Call | $S>K$ |
| Put | $S<K$ |

## Time value is what remains beyond intrinsic value

$$\text{Option premium}=\text{intrinsic value}+\text{time value}$$

Time value reflects the possibility of more favorable outcomes before expiration.

At expiration, time value is zero.

## Long-option loss is capped at the premium

For a call bought at premium $c$:

$$\Pi_{call}=\max(S_T-K,0)-c$$

For a put bought at premium $p$:

$$\Pi_{put}=\max(K-S_T,0)-p$$

The writer receives the mirror-image profit and loss.

| Strategy | Expiration break-even |
|---|---|
| Long call | $K+c$ |
| Long put | $K-p$ |

A 110 put costing 0.625 points breaks even at:

$$110-0.625=109.375=109\text{-}12$$

## Put-call parity prevents inconsistent prices

For European options on a non-coupon-paying cash asset:

$$C-P=S_0-Ke^{-rT}$$

Equivalently:

$$C+Ke^{-rT}=P+S_0$$

Two portfolios with the same expiration payoff must have the same price today.

Thus, a protective put is equivalent to a call plus the present value of the strike:

$$S_0+P=C+Ke^{-rT}$$

For European options on futures, the corresponding parity is:

$$c-p=e^{-rT}(F_0-K)$$

Parity is both a pricing relationship and a map of synthetic positions.

## Six inputs drive option value

| Input rises | Call value | Put value |
|---|---:|---:|
| Underlying price | ↑ | ↓ |
| Strike | ↓ | ↑ |
| Time to expiration | Usually ↑ | Usually ↑ |
| Volatility | ↑ | ↑ |
| Risk-free rate | Usually ↑ | Usually ↓ |
| Coupon or income | ↓ | ↑ |

Effects depend on the exact underlying and model.

## Volatility benefits both option buyers

The option buyer participates in favorable outcomes but can walk away from unfavorable exercise.

- More dispersion raises the value of the right
- Direction does not need to be known in advance
- The writer demands a larger premium

Volatility changes option value even when expected price is unchanged.

## Black–Scholes values an option on a traded asset

For a non-coupon-paying underlying:

$$C=S_0N(d_1)-Ke^{-rT}N(d_2)$$

$$P=Ke^{-rT}N(-d_2)-S_0N(-d_1)$$

$$d_1=\frac{\ln(S_0/K)+(r+\sigma^2/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt{T}},\qquad d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt{T}$$

## A zero-coupon bond option fits the basic formula

Suppose $S_0=95$, $K=94$, $T=0.75$, $r=3\%$, and $\sigma=12\%$.

Using $N(d_1)=0.6444$ and $N(d_2)=0.6050$:

$$C=95(0.6444)-94e^{-0.03(0.75)}(0.6050)$$

$$C\approx5.61$$

The calculation discounts the strike, not the current underlying price.

## Coupon bonds require an income adjustment

Coupons paid before option expiration reduce the value available to the option holder.

A common approximation replaces spot price with:

$$S_0^*=S_0-PV(\text{coupons before expiration})$$

Interest-rate models are preferable when bond price dynamics and curve movements matter materially.

## A binomial tree makes replication visible

Choose up and down factors to match volatility:

$$u=e^{\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}},\qquad d=\frac{1}{u}$$

Risk-neutral probability:

$$q=\frac{e^{r\Delta t}-d}{u-d}$$

Then discount expected option values backward through the tree.

## Backward induction separates payoff from pricing

1. Build terminal underlying prices.
2. Apply $\max(S_T-K,0)$ or $\max(K-S_T,0)$.
3. Form the risk-neutral expected value at each prior node.
4. Discount one step.
5. Repeat to time 0.

American options also compare continuation value with immediate exercise value at each node.

## Implied volatility makes model price equal market price

$$\text{Model price}(\sigma_{impl})=\text{Observed option price}$$

Implied volatility is found by iteration or interpolation.

It is a market-consistent pricing input—not a promise about realized volatility.

## Black's model is built for futures options

$$c=e^{-rT}[F_0N(d_1)-KN(d_2)]$$

$$p=e^{-rT}[KN(-d_2)-F_0N(-d_1)]$$

$$d_1=\frac{\ln(F_0/K)+\tfrac12\sigma^2T}{\sigma\sqrt T},\qquad d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt T$$

Both futures price and strike are inside the discounted payoff.

## A protective put places a floor under bond exposure

A manager long bonds buys puts on Treasury futures.

- Rates rise → bond loses, put gains
- Rates fall → bond gains, put expires
- Premium is the cost of preserving upside

This is insurance against a large adverse rate move, not a free hedge.

## Delta-DV01 sizes an option hedge locally

If portfolio DV01 is \$9,000, put delta magnitude is 0.45, and futures DV01 is \$75:

$$N_p=\frac{9{,}000}{0.45(75)}=266.67$$

Use about 267 puts for the initial local hedge.

Delta changes with futures price, time, and volatility, so the hedge must be monitored.

## Covered calls exchange upside for premium income

Long bond or futures exposure + short call:

- Premium cushions modest losses
- Return improves in flat markets
- Upside is capped above the strike
- Short-option margin and assignment risk remain

Covered calls monetize a willingness to sell upside—not simply “extra yield.”

## Protective puts and covered calls solve opposite problems

| Strategy | Keeps upside? | Limits downside? | Premium cash flow |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Protective put | Yes | Yes, locally | Pay |
| Covered call | No, capped | Only by premium | Receive |

Choose based on the risk objective before comparing premiums.

## Model output is only as good as the mapping

- Yield curves do not move in one dimension
- Futures basis and CTD can change
- Volatility varies by strike and maturity
- Liquidity and transaction costs matter
- American exercise can matter
- Delta and DV01 evolve through time

Practical hedging combines a model with scenarios and implementation judgment.

## An option decision begins with the unwanted outcome

1. Define the underlying exposure and adverse scenario.
2. Choose the option type, contract, expiration, and strike.
3. Translate premium into dollars and break-even.
4. Size with delta-DV01, then stress nonlinear outcomes.
5. Evaluate basis, liquidity, margin, and rebalancing.
6. Compare the hedge with doing nothing or using futures.

## Options buy flexibility; the premium makes the tradeoff explicit

- Calls and puts create asymmetric payoff profiles.
- Intrinsic value and time value explain the premium.
- Parity links option prices and synthetic positions.
- Black–Scholes, binomial, and Black models match different underlyings and exercise features.
- Protective puts preserve upside; covered calls sell it.
- A successful hedge maps the option to the actual fixed-income risk.
